strengths: Proposes a novel pipeline that combines 2D image editing, 3D mesh generation, and Poisson seamless fusion to enable high-fidelity mesh editing.
Introduces a hybrid SDF/Mesh representation with Poisson Geometry Blending and Poisson Texture Harmonization to achieve seamless geometric and appearance integration.
Quantitative results on CLIP_sim, CLIP_dir, NIQE, and NIMA show consistent improvements over baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit).
Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component (geometry blending, texture harmonization, and individual loss terms).
Demonstrates versatility by extending the framework to drag-based mesh editing, showing potential for broader applications.
weaknesses: Evaluation dataset is very small (only 6 objects), which limits the generalizability of the claimed superiority and statistical significance.
Baseline comparisons are limited to a few methods, mostly SDS/MVD-based; other recent mesh editing approaches are not considered.
Key hyperparameters (e.g., λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, σ, γ, δ, ε0, ε1) are not specified, hindering reproducibility.
The method relies heavily on off-the-shelf 2D and 3D generative models, inheriting their limitations and potentially limiting achievable fidelity for complex meshes.
Technical novelty is incremental: Poisson blending is a classical technique, and the contribution primarily lies in adapting it to a hybrid representation.
The claim of being the 'first' framework may be overstated given prior works that combine 2D editing with 3D generation.
No user study is conducted to validate perceptual quality and editing control, which is important for a user-centric editing task.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated pipeline that reframes mesh editing as an 'image editing -> mesh generation -> seamless fusion' process, cleanly separating the strengths of 2D editing models (FLUX Kontext) and 3D generators (MeshyAI) from the fusion problem.

The Joint Geometry and Appearance Fusion is a genuine technical contribution: a hybrid SDF/Mesh representation that applies Poisson normal blending for geometry and Poisson-style gradient/distribution/boundary losses for texture, jointly addressing geometry and appearance rather than radiance fields alone (unlike SeamlessNeRF or 3DGS stitching).

Clear quantitative gains over FocalDreamer, MagicClay, and Instant3dit on all four reported metrics (CLIP_sim, CLIP_dir, NIQE, NIMA), plus convincing qualitative comparisons on insertion, deletion, and complex edits (e.g., removing a volcano while filling the cavity with adjacent-region rocks).

Ablation studies in Fig. 6 and Tab. 2 isolate the effect of Poisson Geometry Blending, Poisson Texture Harmonization, and each loss term (L_distribution, L_grad, L_boundary), providing evidence that the design choices matter.
Demonstrated flexibility beyond text prompts: drag-based mesh editing via LightningDrag, showing the framework can be extended to spatial manipulation tasks without re-architecting.
Generally clear writing, informative pipeline figure (Fig. 2), and explicit acknowledgment of limitations (dependence on off-the-shelf 2D/3D models).
weaknesses: Evaluation is narrow: only six objects are used, with no geometric fidelity metrics (e.g., chamfer distance or normal consistency on unedited regions) to substantiate the central claim of preserving the original fine-scale geometry and texture. The reported metrics (CLIP_sim/CLIP_dir, NIQE, NIMA) are all proxy or no-reference image-quality measures, which are weak evidence for mesh-level fidelity.

The pipeline depends heavily on off-the-shelf components (FLUX Kontext for editing, MeshyAI for image-to-mesh, MagicClay backbone for the SDF representation), so the core novelty is essentially the fusion step; the paper does not quantify how much of the improvement comes from better underlying generative models versus the fusion itself.

No user study is provided, despite the paper repeatedly making perceptual claims ('aesthetically satisfying to human vision', 'high-fidelity colors'), which are the natural way to validate seamless-editing results.

Reproducibility is not fully supported for review: the implementation is only promised 'upon acceptance', and key hyperparameters (lambda_1, lambda_2, theta_1, theta_2, epsilon_0, epsilon_1, delta, sigma, gamma) are stated without values or sensitivity analysis.

The comparison set is limited to three baselines and omits more recent native-3D and mesh-editing methods discussed in related work; the claim of being 'the first framework' to reformulate mesh editing this way is not strongly substantiated.

Failure cases are shown in Fig. 4 (rows labeled 'Fail') but not analyzed, and the limitation section only briefly attributes failures to input complexity without characterizing when or why the fusion breaks (e.g., open surfaces, multi-layer topology).
Details of the drag-based editing evaluation are qualitative only (Fig. 5); no quantitative or systematic comparison is given for this claimed capability.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant and practically important problem—controllable, high-fidelity 3D mesh editing that preserves the original geometry and appearance—which is underserved relative to implicit/NeRF-based editing.

The overall pipeline (2D image edit → edited-region mesh generation → Poisson-based fusion) is a reasonable and coherent engineering recipe, and the proposed Joint Geometry and Appearance Fusion is conceptually well motivated, explicitly targeting both geometric and texture seams rather than only one.
The extension to drag-based editing (via LightningDrag) is a nice demonstration of framework versatility and adds practical value beyond text-only editing.
The paper is generally well organized and clearly written, with informative figures (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) and a sensible loss design for texture harmonization (distribution, gradient, and boundary terms).
The ablation study (Table 2, Fig. 6) isolates the contribution of Geometry Blending, Texture Harmonization, and each loss term, and shows consistent gains over the mesh-Boolean baseline.
weaknesses: Novelty is largely incremental: the method is essentially a composition of off-the-shelf components (FLUX Kontext for 2D editing, MeshyAI for image-to-3D, MagicClay for the hybrid SDF/mesh backbone, LightningDrag for drag editing) glued together with a Poisson blending scheme adapted from classical Poisson Image Editing [37] and SeamlessNeRF [15]. The 'hybrid SDF/mesh' representation is explicitly stated to be inspired by MagicClay [2], and the claim of being 'the first framework' to reformulate mesh editing as an image-edit→mesh-gen→fusion pipeline is an overclaim given prior seamless-editing and mesh-editing literature.

Evaluation is far too thin to support the sweeping claims of superiority. The dataset consists of only six objects, all assessed with automatic metrics. For a paper whose central selling point is high visual fidelity and 'aesthetically satisfying' results, the complete absence of any human/user study is a serious gap, and four automated metrics (CLIP_sim, CLIP_dir, NIQE, NIMA) cannot substitute for perceptual evaluation of seam quality.

Several critical technical details are underspecified. How is the generated edited-region mesh (from MeshyAI) aligned, scaled, and oriented relative to the original mesh so that the Boolean intersection in Eqs. (1)–(2) is meaningful? How is the 'editing region' automatically localized in 3D from a 2D edit? These are the crux of making the pipeline work and are left vague, undermining reproducibility and the claimed controllability.

Reported quantitative gains are modest on some axes (e.g., NIQE 3.203 vs. 3.377; NIMA 5.071 vs. 4.834) and rely on only three baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit), omitting more recent mesh-editing and native-3D editing approaches discussed in related work. The ablation baseline is only mesh Boolean, which is a weak reference point and inflates the apparent improvement.

The authors themselves acknowledge in the Limitation section that the method inherits the failures of its off-the-shelf 2D/3D models and struggles with complex meshes (open surfaces, multiple layers, noisy surfaces). Since these are exactly the cases where an editing method is most needed, this substantially narrows the practical applicability that the paper claims.

Some qualitative results are unconvincing or ambiguous. For example, in Fig. 4 the 'Remove the creature's volcano' row appears to leave residual/ambiguous geometry in the Ours column, and several edited results show visible scale/appearance mismatch, which weakens the 'seamless' and 'high-fidelity' claims. Code is only promised 'upon acceptance,' and the reliance on a proprietary service (MeshyAI) further hinders reproducibility.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem in 3D content creation: controllable, high-fidelity mesh editing while preserving the original mesh structure, which is less explored than neural-field editing.

Proposes a complete and technically reasonable pipeline that combines 2D image editing, 3D generative mesh generation, and seamless fusion. The introduction of Poisson Geometry Blending and Poisson Texture Harmonization is a novel adaptation of Poisson-based fusion to explicit meshes via a hybrid SDF/mesh representation.

Provides quantitative experiments on 100 diverse 3D models with 3 editing prompts, comparing against four recent baselines (FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit, VoxHammer) across CLIP_sim, CLIP_dir, NIQE, and NIMA, with consistent improvements reported in Table 1.

Includes ablation studies that isolate the effects of Geometry Blending, Texture Harmonization, and individual texture losses (gradient, boundary, distribution), with both quantitative results (Table 2) and qualitative visualizations (Figure 6) supporting the design choices.

Demonstrates versatility by extending the framework to drag-based mesh editing and showing qualitative examples (Figure 5), and argues for model-agnosticism by evaluating with Trellis, Hunyuan3D 2.5, and MeshyAI backbones.
The paper is generally well-organized and clearly written, with informative figures (e.g., Figure 2 pipeline overview, Figure 3 geometry blending details) that help explain the method.
weaknesses: The evaluation metrics are not well aligned with the central claims of geometric fidelity and structural consistency. CLIP_sim/CLIP_dir are semantic/image-level metrics, while NIQE/NIMA are no-reference 2D image quality metrics; none directly measures 3D geometry, mesh topology, or seam quality (e.g., Chamfer distance, normal consistency, or texture seam metrics).

No user study is conducted. For mesh editing tasks, human judgment is critical for assessing artifacts such as seams, color shifts, and structural unnaturalness, especially since the quantitative metrics are only indirect proxies.

The evaluation dataset and prompts are constructed by the authors, not a public benchmark. With 100 models and 3 prompts per model, the evaluation is limited in breadth, and results may not be directly comparable to other published mesh-editing methods.

Reproducibility is limited: the main experiments rely on proprietary/commercial components (FLUX Kontext, MeshyAI), and code is not released. Key hyperparameters (λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, δ, γ, σ, sampling counts, number of rendered views, resolution) are not specified, making exact replication difficult.

Some technical claims are not experimentally validated. For example, the assertion that the implicit SDF 'effectively resolves inconsistencies' in blended normal maps is not directly tested, and the claimed extension to PBR materials is not demonstrated with experiments.

Certain formulations raise stability and implementation questions. The boundary weight in Eq. (9) can become unbounded near the boundary, and the KDE-based color distribution loss in Eq. (10) lacks details on color sampling and bandwidth selection, which may affect robustness and reproducibility.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly described pipeline: mesh editing is reformulated as image editing → edited-region mesh generation → seamless fusion, which cleanly decouples the semantic edit (2D editor) from the geometry synthesis (image-to-mesh) and from the fusion, and makes the framework agnostic to both backends (Sec. 3.1, Tab. 2).

Concrete technical contribution in the fusion stage: applying Poisson Image Editing in the 2D rendered normal-map domain and back-propagating through a hybrid SDF/mesh optimization sidesteps the O(n^3) volumetric Poisson solve and the connectivity/gradient-discontinuity problems of classical Poisson mesh editing (Sec. 3.2.1), enabling gradient-domain fusion on explicit meshes, which SeamlessNeRF and GaussianStitching cannot do.

The texture harmonization is well designed and each term is motivated and ablated: gradient propagation for detail preservation, a distance-weighted soft boundary loss for seamless transitions, and a KDE-based distribution-alignment loss that specifically addresses the failure of pure Poisson propagation on repetitive texture patterns (Eqs. 7–12, Fig. 6e–g).

Consistent and large quantitative gains: best on all four metrics (CLIP_sim 20.801, CLIP_dir 18.479, NIQE 4.710, NIMA 5.928) against four baselines (Tab. 1), with qualitative evidence of structural harmony and fine detail where baselines distort geometry or alter unrelated regions (Fig. 4, e.g. the volcano-removal case).

Ablation over three different mesh backbones (Trellis, Hunyuan3D 2.5, MeshyAI) supports the claim that improvements come from the fusion pipeline rather than a single generator, and the drag-based editing extension (Fig. 5) demonstrates genuine versatility beyond prompt-driven edits.
Reasonable implementation transparency: iteration counts, GPU, and per-stage timings (5 min / 1000 iters for geometry, 1 min / 2000 iters for texture) are reported, aiding assessment of practicality.
weaknesses: Evaluation relies entirely on CLIP-based metrics and no-reference IQA (NIQE/NIMA), which are weak proxies for perceptual fidelity and editing success in 3D; no user study is conducted, and the 100-model, 3-prompt dataset is self-constructed from Objaverse-XL/GSO/web rather than a standard public benchmark, limiting comparability with future work.

Potential confounding between backbone strength and the proposed method: baselines are end-to-end editing methods while CraftMesh uses a state-of-the-art image-to-mesh generator (MeshyAI) and a strong 2D editor. The ablation table is ambiguous about which backbone the ablation rows use, and the reported numbers do not unambiguously support the claim that combining both components is best (w/ Geometry Blending alone reports CLIP_sim 20.502, above Ours (Trellis) 19.166 and essentially tied with Ours (MeshyAI) 20.801), contradicting the statement that the best configuration combines both.

Missing comparisons to methods discussed at length in related work, most notably the classical Poisson mesh editing of Yu et al. [56] that this work positions itself against, as well as MVEdit [5], CMD [23], MaskedLRM [14], and neural-field editors; only four baselines are compared.

Key method details are underspecified: how the 3D editing region is determined from the 2D edit (the paper claims no manual 3D region specification is needed, but the mechanism for mapping 2D masks/edits to the 3D region across views is not explained), how the mesh Boolean union/difference behaves on non-watertight, thin, or multi-component geometry, and how multi-view Poisson normal blending is kept consistent across camera viewpoints beyond the assertion that the SDF 'effectively resolves inconsistencies'.

Reproducibility is limited: the project page URL is blank and no code release is indicated; the system depends on proprietary/off-the-shelf components (FLUX Kontext, MeshyAI, LightningDrag), so the end-to-end pipeline cannot be independently verified from the paper alone.
The claim that the texture formulation 'directly extends to physically based rendering (PBR) materials' is not supported by any PBR experiment or result in the paper.

Failure analysis is thin: only two 'Fail' annotations are shown for baselines, with no quantitative failure rates, no analysis of when CraftMesh itself breaks, and only a generic limitation paragraph about complex meshes; also, no comparison of runtime against the baselines is provided despite the added generation/fusion stages.

strengths: The target problem is relevant: high-fidelity, part-level editing of explicit meshes is under-explored relative to neural-field editing, and meshes remain the dominant representation in professional content-creation pipelines, so a working mesh-editing framework has practical value.

The decomposition (2D image edit → region mesh generation → fusion into the original mesh) is sensible and modular, and the paper does show model-agnosticism by swapping the mesh-generation backbone (Trellis, Hunyuan3D 2.5, MeshyAI in Table 2), which is a useful property for a pipeline-style contribution.

Solving the Poisson blend in the 2D rendered-normal domain instead of the 3D volume is a reasonable engineering decision, with a stated complexity reduction from O(n^3) to O(kn^2) (Sec. 3.2.1), and it is consistent with the reported 5-minute/1000-iteration geometry stage.

The ablation study is reasonably structured: Fig. 6 and Table 2 isolate Poisson Geometry Blending, Poisson Texture Harmonization, and the individual gradient/boundary/distribution losses, and each component is shown to change both qualitative artifacts (seams, hue shifts, blur) and the reported metrics.

Qualitative comparisons in Fig. 4 do suggest the method can produce more coherent global structure and finer local detail than FocalDreamer, MagicClay, Instant3dit, and VoxHammer on several prompts, and the drag-based extension (Fig. 5) demonstrates framework flexibility beyond text prompting.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is thin relative to how it is framed. Poisson Image Editing [38] is a 2003 classic, and the hybrid SDF/Mesh representation is explicitly adopted from MagicClay [2] (Sec. 3.2). The remaining new element is applying Poisson blending to rendered normal maps with SDF-based refinement, i.e., a combination of off-the-shelf FLUX Kontext, an image-to-3D service, mesh Booleans, and a classical operator. The abstract's claim of a 'novel framework' with 'state-of-the-art' results overstates this.

The evaluation cannot support the state-of-the-art claim. All four metrics are 2D image-based (CLIP_sim/CLIP_dir on rendered views, NIQE, NIMA). There are no geometry metrics (Chamfer distance, normal consistency, Hausdorff, topology/connectivity preservation), no per-task breakdown for insertion vs. deletion vs. localized editing, no user study despite repeated claims of 'aesthetically satisfying to human vision' and metrics that 'better align with human visual judgment,' and no variance/error bars or significance tests over the 100 models × 3 prompts. NIQE/NIMA are no-reference natural-image metrics of questionable validity for rendered 3D assets.

The comparison is likely confounded. The best configuration ('Ours (MeshyAI)') uses a commercial image-to-3D service and FLUX Kontext, i.e., stronger generative backbones than the baselines use, so gains may come from the components rather than from the proposed fusion. Table 2 only varies backbones for their own method, not for the baselines, and the paper provides no baseline-strength control (e.g., feeding baselines the same edited reference image or the same region mesh).

Reproducibility is inadequate. No values are given for λ1, λ2, θ1, θ2, γ, δ, σ, ε0, ε1, mask thresholds, mesh/SDF resolution, or optimizer settings (learning rate, schedule); only iteration counts are reported. No code, weights, or project page is provided (the abstract's project page is blank), and the 100-model evaluation set and its prompts are self-constructed and not released.

Several core mechanisms are under-specified, making the method hard to assess or reimplement: how the 2D edit mask is lifted to a 3D editing region; how the original mesh and edited region mesh are aligned (reference [58] is cited with no detail); how the SDF and explicit mesh are coupled during 'indirect optimization'; and how the SDF is trained from the blended normals with what regularization weights.

The Poisson formulation is theoretically loose. Eq. 4 simply writes n_p = Γ(n_t, n_e, mask^opt), without explaining why the mask boundary in each rendered view coincides with the actual 3D fusion seam, and the authors themselves note that the blended normal maps are 'not strictly multi-view consistent,' then assert that 'the implicit SDF effectively resolves inconsistencies' with no supporting experiment. Similarly, the claim that the texture formulation 'directly extends to physically based rendering (PBR) materials' is asserted with no PBR experiment.

Failure cases are visible but unanalyzed. Fig. 4 contains 'Fail' labels (including near the authors' own column) that are never discussed, and the limitation section only vaguely mentions 'complex meshes (open, multiple layers, noisy surfaces)' without quantifying when the mesh-Boolean-based region extraction or SDF fitting breaks.

Related-work positioning is shallow and partly unsupported. The blanket statement that MVD-based editing methods 'fail to preserve the geometry and texture of the original model' is asserted without citation or evidence, and the 'Seamless Editing' discussion does not clearly distinguish the proposed normal-domain Poisson blending from SeamlessNeRF [16], which also performs Poisson-based blending and is dismissed only because it operates in radiance fields.

Presentation problems compound the above: Fig. 2/Fig. 3 have overlapping, ambiguous panels and labels (e.g., 'Generated Texture' vs. 'Training Texture', the direction of the 'Poisson Image Editing' arrow), Fig. 3 is described in the text as 'an overview of the workflow' while its caption says 'Details of Poisson Geometry Blending,' and the figure grids (Fig. 4, Fig. 6) are difficult to map to the claims in the text.
